key_insight: The paper shows that robots can learn a lightweight, task-relevant memory during training using saliency-guided supervision, instead of repeatedly running expensive VLM queries at inference time. This makes long-horizon manipulation more practical by keeping only the information that matters for the task.
problem_solved: Robotic policies often need memory of past events to succeed on long manipulation tasks, but using full histories can introduce noise and spurious correlations. Existing memory methods may also be too expensive because they rely on VLM calls during execution.
method: Use computationally expensive VLM queries during training to identify which past events are task-salient.
Train a compact workspace memory model to store only the most relevant historical information.
Deploy the learned memory at test time so the robot can condition on concise, meaningful state instead of full history or repeated VLM inference.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this offers a more efficient way to add memory to robotic policies without the runtime cost of large vision-language models. It can improve robustness on long-horizon tasks while reducing latency and deployment complexity.

paper_title: Workspace Models: Lightweight Robotic Memory via Saliency-Driven Supervision
paper_authors: Nitish Dashora, Douglas Chen, Idan Shenfeld, John Marangola, Pulkit Agrawal
